newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo may review its growth targets - minister.
newsitem.headline: Yugo may review its growth targets - minister.

text.p: Yugoslavia may have to reassess its 1997 growth targets after some assumptions on which it relied for this year's growth failed to materialise, the minister for Development, Science and Environment said on Friday.
"In regard to quantitative indicators the federal government will reassess possibilities for their realisation as planned," Jagos Zelenovic told a news conference.
Yugoslavia ambitiously set its 1997 growth targets, seeing its GDP growing 13 percent, industry up 14 percent and exports rising almost 47 percent.

It was widely assumed that Yugoslavia would rejoin the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and World Trade Organisation and normalise ties with London club and Paris club creditors, the European Union and ex-Yugoslav states.
Repaired ties with world financial bodies were expected to lead Yugoslavia back to international markets and allow Belgrade to restructure and reschedule its external debt, Zelenovic said.
"But despite efforts, no substantial progress has been made and there are no results. Those will remain the key limits to the economic policy in the second half of 1997," he said.
January-June statistics showed industry grew 7.6 percent and exports were 28.5 percent up on the same period 1996.

But the government will not change its key economic policy goals -- price and currency stability, production and exports growth, structural changes, privatisation and improvement in the standards of living, Zelenovic said.

"The key economic policy concepts and goals are the same. We do not say they will be realised and we do not say they will not... But the government will reassess real possibilities of those quantifications to materialise," he said.
Last week, Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic said the federal government firmly stood by the set economic targets and that it would not revise them for a single percent.
Yugoslavia also hoped that effects from a set of reform laws adopted in the first half of the year will be felt by the end of 1997.

"The government will speed up reforms, privatisation, structural changes and further liberalise foreign trade regime. Priority will be to further intensify production and exports along with maintaining price and currency stability," Zelenovic said.

Beside external limits, Yugoslavia's economy was facing many internal problems, mainly lack of working capital, widespread dinar illiquidity of companies and banks, lack of savings and huge inter-company debt, the minister said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
